en.name: Mint, fresh
en.summary: Fresh mint keeps 1–2 weeks at room temperature with its stems in water, or 2–3 weeks in the fridge at 4 °C (40 °F) or below. It is sturdier than coriander or basil, which is why it gets the longer window of the soft herbs.
en.pantry: 1–2 weeks with the stems trimmed and standing in a couple of centimetres of water, out of direct sun, changing the water daily. Mint is a tougher leaf than most soft herbs and takes to this treatment well — a bunch in a glass on the worktop will often root itself given a fortnight, which tells you how happy it is. Do not cover the leaves tightly; trapped humidity around the leaf is what turns a bunch black from the inside out.
en.fridge: 2–3 weeks at 4 °C (40 °F) or below, wrapped loosely in dry kitchen paper inside a bag or box in the crisper, or with the stems in a jar of water and a loose bag over the top. Do not wash it until you use it. Go through the bunch every few days and pull out any blackened leaf, because one rotting leaf will take the ones touching it. Mint bruises easily, so keep it where nothing heavy will sit on top of it.
en.freezer: Freeze damage will appear, so no freezer timeline is given. Whole mint leaves come out of the freezer dark and limp, with no structure left. The way that does work is to chop the leaves and freeze them in an ice-cube tray with water — perfect for dropping into a jug of tea or a cold drink — or to blitz them with a little oil for cooking. For a garnish, only fresh will do.
en.thawing: Do not thaw. Drop mint ice cubes straight into a drink, or frozen chopped mint straight into the pan.
spoilage: Blackened, translucent leaves that have gone slimy.
A sour or musty smell rather than a clean, cooling one.
Slime at the cut ends or cloudy water in the jar.
Mould on the stems, particularly where they sat in stale water.
tips: Stand a bunch in water on the counter; mint responds better to this than most herbs.
Change the water daily and re-trim the stems.
Pick off blackened leaves promptly; one bad leaf spreads.
Freeze chopped mint in ice cubes for drinks rather than freezing whole leaves.

faq.q: How long does fresh mint keep?
faq.a: 1–2 weeks at room temperature with the stems in water, or 2–3 weeks in the fridge at 4 °C (40 °F) or below.
Freeze damage will appear, so no timeline is given. Whole leaves go dark and limp; chopped mint frozen in ice cubes is genuinely useful for drinks.

faq.q: How do you stop mint going black?
faq.a: Keep the leaves dry and give them air. Stems in water with a loose bag, or a dry paper wrap in a box, and never wash it until you use it.

zh.name: 新鮮薄荷
zh.summary: 新鮮薄荷把莖插在水裡放常溫可放 1～2 週，放 4 °C 以下冷藏則是 2～3 週。它比香菜或羅勒強韌，所以在軟莖香草裡拿到比較長的窗口。
zh.pantry: 把莖剪一下、插進約兩公分深的水裡，放在不直曬的地方，每天換水，1～2 週。薄荷的葉子比多數軟莖香草結實，也很吃這一套——一束插在檯面上杯子裡的薄荷，兩週後常常就自己長根了，可見它有多自在。葉子不要包緊；困在葉片周圍的濕氣，正是讓一整把薄荷從裡面黑起來的原因。
zh.fridge: 放 4 °C 以下 2～3 週：用乾的廚房紙巾鬆鬆包好、裝進袋子或盒子放蔬果室；或把莖插進水杯、上面鬆罩一個袋子。要用時才洗。每隔幾天翻一下，把發黑的葉子挑掉，因為一片爛葉會把貼著它的那幾片一起拖下水。薄荷容易壓傷，請放在不會被重物壓到的位置。
zh.freezer: 冷凍會出現凍傷，所以沒有給期限。整片薄荷葉從冷凍拿出來又深又軟，結構完全沒了。真正可行的做法是把葉子切碎、加水用製冰盒凍成塊——丟進一壺茶或冷飲裡剛剛好——或加一點油打成泥供料理使用。要擺盤的話，只有新鮮的能用。
zh.thawing: 不要解凍。薄荷冰塊直接丟進飲料，冷凍碎薄荷直接下鍋。
spoilage: 葉子發黑、變透明、摸起來黏滑。
聞起來酸或有霉味，而不是乾淨的清涼氣味。
切口變黏滑，或杯子裡的水變混濁。
莖上長霉，尤其是泡在放久的水裡那一段。
tips: 整束插水放檯面上；薄荷對這個做法的反應比多數香草都好。
每天換水，並重新剪一下莖。
發黑的葉子要盡快挑掉；一片壞的會擴散。
把切碎的薄荷做成冰塊冷凍給飲料用，不要整片冷凍。

faq.a: 莖插水放常溫 1～2 週，或 4 °C 以下冷藏 2～3 週。
冷凍會凍傷，所以沒有給期限。整片葉子會變深變軟；切碎做成冰塊冷凍，給飲料用倒是真的好用。
讓葉子保持乾燥並且透氣。莖插水、上面鬆罩袋子，或用乾紙巾包好放盒子，而且要用時才洗。
